### Libraries

```{r}
library(bayesrules)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)
library(plotly)
library(report)
```

### Intro

Welcome to today's lecture, we will analyze Capital Bikeshare Data from Washington D.C

```{r}
bikes_data <- bayesrules::bikes
```

Starter Questions:

1.  What is the distribution of ridership? Make a histogram and write what you see below

```{r}
library(bayesrules)
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = rides)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", bins = 10) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Daily Bikeshare Ridership",
       x = "Number of Rides per Day", y = "Number of Days")
```

This graph just shows that there's a lot of day-to-day variation in ridership, which tells me that something else (like weather or season) is influencing how many people ride bikes.

2.  Has ridership increased over time? Make a plot and write what you see below

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = date, y = rides)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Ridership Over Time",
       x = "Date", y = "Number of Rides")
```

This is graph shows that I was right with my assumption of the weather or season being a factor to the number of riders. As you could see, it rises during spring/summer and falls in winter (repeating across both years.

3.  Are there more rides on weekdays or weekends? Make a plot and write what you see below

```{r}

library(plotly)

bikes_summary <- bikes_data %>%
  group_by(weekend) %>%
  summarize(avg_rides = mean(rides))

riders <- ggplot(bikes_summary, aes(x = weekend, y = avg_rides)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Average Ridership: Weekday vs. Weekend",
       x = "Weekend?", y = "Average Number of Rides")

ggplotly(riders, tooltip = "text")
```

4.  **Does temperature feel effect ridership**?

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_feel, y = rides)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_feel, y = rides)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  stat_cor()
  
```

What is a correlation coefficient and p value: [helpful tool here](https://rpsychologist.com/correlation/)

R = 0.58 — the strength and direction of the pattern you're looking at

- On the -1-to-1 scale, 0.58 sits in **moderate** territory: real and clearly visible in the scatter, but the cloud of points still has meaningful width around the line, not tightly hugging it the way an R of 0.9+ would.

Squaring it tells you something more concrete about the plot: R² ≈ 0.34

- About **34% of the vertical scatter in ridership** across this plot is explained by where a point sits on the x-axis (temperature). The remaining **66%** is everything else the plot doesn't capture

p \< 2.2×10⁻¹⁶ — how confident you should be that this pattern is real, not a fluke of these particular 500 days

- This tests rhe hypothesis that temperature and ridership have *no* linear relationship at all in the underlying population, and this pattern is just coincidental noise from sampling 500 particular days. The p-value says: **if that null hypothesis were actually true, seeing a correlation as strong as 0.58 in a sample this size would be astronomically unlikely**

```{r}
lm(data = bikes_data, rides~temp_feel)
```

**`(Intercept)` = -2179.27**: the model's predicted ridership when temp_feel = 0. As flagged before, this is a real number the formula produces, but not a practically meaningful one — 0°F essentially never happens in D.C., so this is just "where the line would cross the y-axis if you extended it that far," not a usable prediction.

**`temp_feel` = 81.88**: the slope — for every one-unit (one degree) increase in temp_feel, the model predicts ridership increases by 81.88 rides. This is the number that actually answers "does temperature matter, and by how much"

```{r}

model <- lm(rides ~ temp_feel, data = bikes_data)
report(model)
```

### Your turn

Repeat the all the steps to model the relationship between

rides and humidity

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = humidity, y = rides)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = humidity, y = rides)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  stat_cor()
```

R = -0.069 — On the -1-to-1 scale, this is a very weak, negative relationship (basically close to zero)

R² ≈ 0.005 — about 0.5% of the variation in ridership is explained by humidity. The other 99.5% is everything else.

p = 0.122 — If p \< 0.05, we can’t rule out that it’s just noise. There isn't evidence that humidity has a real linear relationship with ridership.

```{r}
lm(data = bikes_data, rides~humidity)
```

**`(Intercept)` = 3933.722**: the predicted ridership when humidity = 0%. This isn’t practically meaningful, because D.C. basically never has 0% humidity.

**`humidity` = -7.177**: for every 1-point increase in humidity, the model predicts ridership changes by 7.18 rides. That's a tiny effect since p = 0.122, it isn't statistically significant.

```{r}
model_humidity <- lm(rides ~ humidity, data = bikes_data)
report(model_humidity)
```

- rides and windspeed

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = windspeed, y = rides)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = windspeed, y = rides)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  stat_cor()
```

R = -0.19 — On the -1-to-1 scale, this is a weak, negative relationship. Fewer rides on windier days, yet points are still very spread out around the line.

R² ≈ 0.036 — about 3.6% of the variation in ridership is explained by windspeed. The other 96.4% is everything else.

p = 1.13e-05 — Since p \< 0.05, the relationship windspeed and ridership is statistically significant.

```{r}
lm(data = bikes_data, rides~windspeed)
```

**intercept = 4205.06**: On a day with no wind, the model predicts about 4,205 rides.

**Windspeed = -55.52**: For every 1 mph more wind, there are about 56 fewer rides.

```{r}
model_wind <- lm(rides ~ windspeed, data = bikes_data)
report(model_wind)
```

- rides and temp_actual

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_actual, y = rides)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_actual, y = rides)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  stat_cor()
```

R = 0.58 — There’s a moderate, positive relationship.

R² ≈ 0.34 — Temperature explains about **34%** of why ridership goes up and down. The other **66%** comes from other things.

p = 2.2e- 16 — This is **less than 0.05**, so the pattern is **real.**

```{r}
lm(data = bikes_data, rides~temp_actual)
```

(intercept) = -2168.77 : At **0°F**, the model predicts about **-2,169 rides**.

temp_actual = 89.23: For every **1 degree warmer**, there are about **89 more rides**.

```{r}
model_actual <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual, data = bikes_data)
report(model_actual)
```

- temp_feel and temp_actual

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_actual, y = temp_feel)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{r}
ggplot(bikes_data, aes(x = temp_actual, y = temp_feel)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  stat_cor()
```

R = 0.98 — There’s a very strong**, positive** relationship.

R² ≈ 0.96 — Actual temperature explains about **96%** of why the feels-like temperature goes up and down. The other **4%** comes from other things, like humidity and wind.

p = 2.2e- 16 — This is **less than 0.05**, so the pattern is **real.**

```{r}
lm(data = bikes_data, temp_feel~temp_actual)
```

(Intercept) = **0.6223**: When it’s **0°F outside**, the model says it **feels like about 0.6°F**. Basically the same.

temp_actual = **1.082**: Every time it gets **1 degree warmer**, it **feels about 1 degree warmer** too.

```{r}
model_temps <- lm(temp_feel ~ temp_actual, data = bikes_data)
report(model_temps)
```
